request.query: How many days or weeks did you wait for a International House Helsinki appointment for Strong electronic identification (online banking codes) in Helsinki, and how long until it was done?
request.objective: Forum posts, Reddit threads, blogs and university guides from people who did "Strong electronic identification (online banking codes)" (International House Helsinki) in Helsinki, Finland: how long they waited for an appointment or for the result, and appointment availability.

results.title: Bank account in Finland – online banking codes
results.author: VOR Media Technologies
highlights:
In Finland the bank account and the online banking codes (verkkopankkitunnukset) that come with it are two different things. The codes are the everyday electronic identity: they log you in to Suomi.fi e-Identification, the shared login for public e-services, and so to Kela (Social Insurance Institution), Vero (Tax Administration) and the police. Opening a bank account in Finland is a legal right for anyone legally resident in the EEA, and strong identification can be refused only on narrow grounds. The rules are national, set in the Act on Credit Institutions and supervised by the Financial Supervisory Authority (Finanssivalvonta).

...

Bring a passport, a foreigner's identity card or another official identity document; InfoFinland, the authorities' joint guidance service, is blunt that a driving licence will not do, and each bank decides which documents it accepts. Some banks also accept an alien's passport or a refugee travel document issued by a Finnish authority. Opening an account takes an in-person appointment, says the City of Helsinki's Newcomer's Guide. By law the bank must know its customer: it will ask what the account is for, may check your credit history, and may not open the account if you do not answer.

...

A deposit bank that offers payment services must offer a euro perusmaksutili (basic payment account) to every consumer legally resident in an EEA state, on equal terms and without discrimination. It may refuse essentially only for anti-money-laundering reasons, such as an identity it cannot verify. Under chapter 15, section 6 of the Act on Credit Institutions it must accept or reject your application at the latest within ten banking days, and a refusal must be explained in writing, free of charge, together with how to appeal.

...

Because the law treats them separately. The requirements for online banking credentials are stricter than for the account, so some newcomers leave the branch with an account and no codes. A bank may refuse strong electronic identification – codes that work in other services, not only its own – if, for example, you have no Finnish personal identity code or are not in the Population Information System. It must then offer a limited electronic ID for its own services; once your code and registration are in place, ask again. Codes used for Suomi.fi must be issued personally to you and be suitable for other services.

...

The ID card is the alternative worth planning for. The police issue a foreigner's identity card if your identity can be reliably verified, you hold a valid residence permit, residence card or registered right of residence, and you have a kotikunta (municipality of residence) and are entered in the Population Information System. It proves your identity in Finland – at the bank, for instance – but is not a travel document; it is usually valid for five years and expires if your permit or registration is cancelled. Apply online with Suomi.fi identification or at any police station; the helpline for appointments is +358 (0)295 419 800, Monday to Friday 8.00–16.15. In Helsinki, newcomers go to the Helsinki Police Department at Pasilanraitio 11, not to International House Helsinki.

...

## What to do now

| Step | What | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Get your henkilötunnus and DVV registration (part 3) | Before you book the bank |
| 2 | Book an in-person appointment; bring your passport or foreigner's ID card | Your first week |
| 3 | Answer the know-your-customer questions; ask for codes usable in other services | At the appointment |
| 4 | If refused: ask for the reason in writing and a limited e-ID | When the bank answers – at most ten banking days |
| 5 | Apply for the foreigner's ID card as a second token (€53 online) | Once you have a kotikunta |
| 6 | Activate a mobile certificate, then MobilePay | When the codes work |

results.title: First 30 Days in Finland: The Complete Expat Checklist | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
The henkilötunnus is issued by the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency) when you register as a foreign national. There are two steps: submit the online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi, then attend an in-person appointment at a DVV service point.

The in-person appointment is the bottleneck. Wait times vary — in Helsinki they can stretch to a few weeks during busy periods. Book the appointment the day you land, even if you submit the form later.

...

Book an in-person appointment — walk-ins are rarely accepted. Expect a wait of a few days to a week. During the appointment, the bank will also issue your pankkitunnukset (online banking credentials), which is a separate and critical item covered below.

...

Pankkitunnukset are the Finnish online banking login credentials used as a strong electronic identification method. In Finland, these credentials are not just for banking — they are how you log in to:

- OmaKela (Kela's self-service portal)
- OmaVero (tax administration portal at vero.fi)
- Suomi.fi (the national digital services hub)
- Most municipal and public authority portals

When you open your bank account, specifically ask the bank to set up online banking (verkkopankki) and issue you a code calculator or mobile authentication app. Without pankkitunnukset, you cannot complete weeks 3 and 4 of this checklist.

...

Apply in person at a DVV service point. Processing takes 2–4 weeks, which is why you apply in week 4 rather than waiting. The card will arrive within your first two months if you apply now.

...

DVV appointment wait is too long. DVV service point wait times vary significantly by city. Helsinki is the worst; Espoo, Vantaa, and smaller cities are often faster. If you have flexibility, check DVV's online booking system for all service points within commuting distance and book at whichever has the earliest slot.

results.title: How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland? - Finland Handbook
results.author: Finland Handbook Editorial Team
highlights:
However, for EU citizens or those who didn't receive a code with their permit, the process involves a visit to the DVV. In 2026, the standard processing time for a Personal Identity Code at the DVV is generally 1 to 3 weeks after your appointment. The real challenge is often securing the appointment itself. In major cities like Helsinki, Espoo, or Tampere, the "wait for the wait" can be significant. You might find that the first available slot for identity verification is three weeks away, and only after that does the 1–3 week processing clock begin. Understanding Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare is essential here, as this code is the bedrock of your entire administrative life in Finland.

| Application Path | Typical Processing Time | Key Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residence Permit (Migri) | Linked to permit (1–6 months) | Applied for abroad or at Migri |
| EU Citizen (DVV) | 1–3 weeks after appointment | Valid passport & proof of work/study |
| Nordic Citizen (DVV) | 1 week | Personal appearance at DVV |
| Temporary Worker (Short-term) | 1–2 weeks | Finnish employer's confirmation |

...

The most pressing question for most is: what do I do while I wait? It feels like life is on hold. You cannot easily get a Finnish bank account, which in turn means you cannot get "Strong Electronic Identification" (bank IDs) to log into government services. During this gap, you are in a state of administrative limbo. For everyday needs, you can often use your foreign passport for basic things, but for services like healthcare, it becomes tricky. Public health centers usually require a Personal Identity Code to create a patient record in their digital systems.

...

To ensure you get your code as fast as possible, you need to be proactive rather than reactive. The moment you know your move-in date, or the moment you receive your residence permit, check the DVV’s online booking system. Do not wait until you land in Finland to see what’s available. Appointments fill up weeks in advance. If you see no appointments in Helsinki, widen your search radius. The train system in Finland is excellent, and a one-hour trip to a neighboring town could save you three weeks of waiting in the city.

results.title: DVV Registration Finland: Get Your Henkilötunnus (2026) | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
How long

2–3 weeks (work/study) or 3–4 weeks (other cases), from your in-person visit

...

DVV registration in Finland is how a foreigner enters the Population Information System and receives a henkilötunnus (personal identity code) that banks, the tax office and Kela rely on. You register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency by submitting an online registration form, then attending one in-person appointment within a month. It is free and takes roughly two to four weeks.

...

Register with DVV in two stages: submit the free online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration (no authentication needed), then visit a DVV service point in person within 1 month with your passport, residence permit or EU registration certificate, and proof of work or study. Processing then takes 2–3 weeks for work and study cases, 3–4 weeks otherwise. There is no fee — the registration and your henkilötunnus (personal identity code) are completely free.

...

### Step 2 — Book an in-person appointment within one month

After the form, you must visit a DVV service point in person, and you must do so within one month of submitting. The in-person step is non-negotiable — it is where DVV verifies your identity against your documents. Appointments at the busy Helsinki-area locations can fill up, so book as early as you can rather than leaving it to the end of the one-month window.

...

### Step 4 — Wait for processing

Processing time, according to DVV, is roughly 2–3 weeks for work and study registrations and 3–4 weeks for other cases, counted from your visit date. At the end you receive your personal identity code, and DVV separately decides your municipality of residence.

...

For anyone in the capital region, the standout resource is International House Helsinki (ihhelsinki.fi), a single building where DVV, the Tax Administration, Kela, and other authorities share a service point aimed specifically at international newcomers. It is designed to let you handle registration, tax card, and social-insurance steps in roughly one visit rather than several, and the staff are used to dealing with people in English. Many international employers and universities also have HR or student-services teams who shepherd new arrivals through DVV registration — ask, because they often know the local quirks.

...

1. Before or on arrival — settle your residence basis with Migri (permit for non-EU; right-of-residence registration for EU citizens staying over three months).
2. First days — submit the DVV foreigner registration form online and book the in-person appointment.
3. Within the first month — attend the DVV appointment with your documents; this is also a good moment to use International House Helsinki if you are in the capital region.
4. Weeks two to four — DVV processes the registration (2–3 weeks for work/study, 3–4 weeks otherwise) and assigns your personal identity code and, where eligible, your municipality of residence.
5. Once you have the henkilötunnus — open a Finnish bank account, order a tax card from Vero, and register with Kela.
6. Whenever you move permanently or for over 3 months — file a notification of move within one week.

results.title: Best Bank Accounts in Finland for Expats (2026) | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
Once your account is open, the codes are the prize. As Suomi.fi explains, online banking codes must be issued personally to you and are obtained by entering into a contract with a Finnish bank. They are overwhelmingly the most-used way Finnish residents log in to public services online.

A few things to know:

- They are not automatic with the account. Especially for newcomers, the strong-identification step can lag behind account opening — the exact gap the FIN-FSA review flagged. Ask at your appointment specifically when and how you will receive your codes.
- There are alternatives. Finland also recognises the mobile certificate (mobiilivarmenne, a chip-based identity tied to your SIM, offered by mobile operators), certificate cards, and the Finnish Authenticator app. If bank codes are slow, mobiilivarmenne can be a useful second route into Suomi.fi services.
- Joint accounts have a quirk. Per Suomi.fi, online banking codes for a joint account can be used only by the person in whose name the account is held — so each adult generally needs their own codes.

...

Done in this order, you avoid the most common failure mode: assuming the account and the codes arrive together, and being stuck unable to log in to public services for weeks. For the step-by-step mechanics
